0.title: Skill for Living in the Fear of the Lord
0.overview:
Most of us know clever people who make a mess of their lives, and plain people who handle life remarkably well. The difference is not intelligence, education or experience on their own. The Bible calls it wisdom. A person can hold a doctorate and be a fool, and a person who never finished school can be wise. Wisdom is not how much you know. It is knowing how to live.

Scripture gives wisdom a great deal of space. Whole books are devoted to it: Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, many of the Psalms and the letter of James. Jesus taught in parables and proverbs, and ended his greatest sermon with a story about a wise builder and a foolish one. Paul prayed that believers would be filled with all spiritual wisdom and understanding (Col 1:9). Wisdom is not an optional extra for unusually thoughtful Christians. It is part of ordinary obedience.

And the Bible's teaching on wisdom has a surprise at its centre. Wisdom is not finally a set of principles but a person. Paul calls Jesus Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), the one in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3). To grow in wisdom is to grow in Christ.

A working definition may help as we begin. Biblical wisdom is the God-given skill of living well in God's world: seeing life as God sees it, and then choosing and speaking and acting in a way that fits his character, his word and the situation in front of you. It begins with the fear of the LORD, it is learned from Scripture, it grows through prayer, counsel, correction and experience, and it shows itself in a humble and peaceable life.

Nine units: (1) What Wisdom Is; (2) Christ, the Wisdom of God; (3) Two Ways: Wisdom and Folly; (4) How Wisdom Grows; (5) Wise and Foolish Lives in Scripture; (6) Wisdom for Everyday Life; (7) Passing Wisdom On: Parents and Children; (8) The Limits of Wisdom and the Rest of Faith; (9) Proverbs to Memorize. Each unit ends with questions for reflection, and the examples move from the world of the Bible into the kind of situations most of us face every week. The last unit gathers key proverbs onto a single page to learn by heart.

1.title: What Wisdom Is: Skill for Living in God's World
1.overview:
The Old Testament word usually translated wisdom is hokmah, and its range is wider than we might expect. When God gave Moses instructions for the priests' garments, he said to speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill (Exod 28:3). Skill there is the word for wisdom. Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle, was filled with the Spirit of God with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship (Exod 31:3), and ability is the same word again. In the Bible a tailor or a metalworker could be wise. Wisdom is skill: knowing how to make something well.

Biblical wisdom is the skill of making a life well. It is the ability to take what God has said and live it out in the untidy details of real days: a marriage, a workplace, a budget, a conflict, a grief, a decision with no clear rule attached. Knowledge knows that God commands honesty. Wisdom knows how to be honest with a grieving friend, a difficult boss or a teenage son, and when to speak and when to wait.

And all of it begins in one place. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Prov 1:7). The same truth is repeated in Proverbs 9:10, Psalm 111:10 and Job 28:28, as if Scripture wants to make sure we do not miss it. The fear of the LORD is not terror of a cruel master. It is reverent awe before the holy God who made us and to whom we will give account, an awe that leads to trust, worship and obedience. Wisdom starts there because God is the one who made the world and knows how it works. To try to live well while ignoring him is like trying to use a complicated machine after throwing away the maker's instructions.

This means wisdom is first spiritual and only then practical. The Bible's wise person is not mainly the person with good tips for life. It is the person who has bowed before God and so begins to see everything else in its proper light.
1.theology:
Wisdom begins with God: For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding (Prov 2:6). Wisdom is not something we generate from inside ourselves. It is received from God, through his word, by people who come to him humbly. That is why the most gifted person can be a fool and the simplest believer can be wise.

Wisdom and knowledge: Scripture values knowledge, but it never treats knowledge as enough. Paul warns that knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Cor 8:1). Knowledge is what you know; wisdom is knowing what to do with it before God and for the good of others.

Wisdom and obedience: Moses told Israel that keeping God's law will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples (Deut 4:6). Wisdom and obedience are not two different things. A life ordered by God's word is the wise life, and a life that drifts from it, however sophisticated, is the foolish one.

Wisdom and character: James asks, Who is wise and understanding among you? and answers, By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom (Jas 3:13). The proof of wisdom is not an impressive argument but a humble, gentle, good life.
1.examples:
Then: The craftsmen who built the tabernacle were not priests or prophets. They cut stones, carved wood and wove cloth. Yet Scripture says God filled them with wisdom for the work (Exod 31:1-6). Their skill was a gift of the Spirit, used for the worship of God. Wisdom is not reserved for the pulpit or the study. It belongs in the workshop, the kitchen and the office.

Now: Think of two people facing the same news: a job offer in another city, with more money but less time for church and family. One asks only, "What will I gain?" The other asks, "What will this do to my soul, my marriage, my children and my service of Christ? What do the people who know me best think? What has God said about money, contentment and priorities?" Both may be intelligent. Only the second is beginning to think wisely, because only the second is starting with God.

A simple test: When you face a decision, notice which question comes first in your mind. If it is "What do I want?" you are beginning where folly begins. If it is "What would please God here?" you are standing at the beginning of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the motto of the whole book of Proverbs, set at the front door so that every reader passes through it. The fear of the LORD is the beginning, not in the sense of a first step you leave behind, but in the sense of the foundation everything else stands on. And notice the other half of the verse. The opposite of the wise person is not the uneducated person but the one who will not be taught: fools despise wisdom and instruction. In Scripture folly is not a lack of brains. It is a moral choice, the refusal to let God and his word correct you.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill, that they make Aaron's garments to consecrate him for my priesthood. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse quietly widens our idea of wisdom. The people Moses was to speak to were tailors and embroiderers, and God calls them the skillful, men he had filled with a spirit of skill. Both words translate the ordinary Hebrew word for wisdom. Their wisdom was seen in well-made garments. That is the Bible's way of saying that wisdom is practical. It is not floating ideas but good work, rightly done, for God's glory. A Christian nurse who treats patients with competence and kindness, or a mechanic who does honest work, is showing a kind of wisdom God gives and values.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding; yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Look at the verbs a father uses as he teaches his son: receive, treasure up, making your ear attentive, call out, raise your voice, seek it like silver, search for it as for hidden treasures. Wisdom does not fall on the lazy. It is found by people who want it badly enough to dig. Yet the passage ends not with human effort but with divine gift: For the LORD gives wisdom. Both are true. We search with all our heart, and when we find wisdom we discover that God was giving it all along. Effort and grace are not enemies in the Christian life.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James refuses to let wisdom stay in the head. If you claim to be wise, he says, show it, and show it by good conduct done in the meekness of wisdom. That last phrase is striking. True wisdom is meek. It does not need to win every argument or display how much it knows. Some of the wisest Christians you will ever meet are quiet people whose wisdom you notice only over years, in the way they handle trouble, forgive wrongs and give counsel when asked. The loud and self-assured are often less wise than they sound.

1.reflection:
Before reading this unit, how would you have defined wisdom? How does the idea of wisdom as "skill for living" change that?

Why do you think Scripture repeats that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom? What does it look like to fear God in ordinary life?

Think of the wisest person you know personally. What makes them wise? How much of it is knowledge, and how much is character?

In which area of your life do you most need practical, God-given skill right now?

2.title: Christ, the Wisdom of God
2.overview:
The Old Testament searches for wisdom. Job asks, But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? (Job 28:12). Proverbs pictures wisdom as a woman calling in the streets. Solomon was given wisdom beyond any king before him, and yet he finished badly. The long story of Israel shows that even the wisest human beings could not live the wise life consistently. Wisdom was promised, sought and glimpsed, but never fully embodied.

Then Jesus came. As a boy he increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man (Luke 2:52). As a man he taught with such authority that crowds were astonished, and he silenced every trap his enemies set. He said of himself, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42). The queen of Sheba had travelled from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon. Now the true King, wiser than Solomon, was walking the roads of Galilee.

But the deepest wisdom of God was revealed at the place that looked most foolish. To the Jews of Paul's day a crucified Messiah was a contradiction, and to the Greeks it was nonsense. Yet Paul writes, we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:23-24). At the cross God did what no human wisdom could have imagined: he upheld his justice and saved sinners at the same time, by bearing the punishment himself in his Son.

So Christian wisdom is not first a technique. It is a relationship. Christ became to us wisdom from God (1 Cor 1:30). To be united to him by faith is to have the wisdom of God as your own, and to spend the rest of your life learning to think and live like him.
2.theology:
Christ is our wisdom: Paul says Christ became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). Wisdom here is not a separate gift beside salvation. It is the whole saving plan of God, received in Christ. A believer who knows almost nothing else knows the wisest thing in the universe: that God saves sinners through his crucified and risen Son.

All the treasures: In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3). Paul wrote this to a church tempted by teachers who offered deeper secrets beyond Christ. Every claim to a higher wisdom outside Christ is a step down, not up.

Proverbs 8 and Christ: In Proverbs 8 wisdom speaks as a person who was with God before creation, like a master workman (Prov 8:30). Christians have read this in two main ways. Some take it as a direct description of the eternal Son before his incarnation. Others take it as a poetic picture of God's own wisdom, personified as a woman to make it vivid, which the New Testament then shows to be fully embodied in Christ, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Col 1:16). The second reading is the more likely: the chapter is poetry about an attribute of God, and its language should not be pressed into a statement about the Son's origin. In the fourth century some used The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work (Prov 8:22) to argue that Christ was a created being. The church rightly rejected that, because the Son is eternal God. But the line from Proverbs 8 to Christ is real. Everything said there of God's wisdom is perfectly true of him.
2.examples:
Then: The queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with hard questions, and Solomon answered them all (1 Kgs 10:1-3). She left overwhelmed. Jesus used her as a rebuke to his own generation, who had something far greater on their doorstep and did not come to listen. People still travel far, read widely and pay dearly for wisdom, while leaving the Gospels unopened on a shelf.

Now: A young believer at university is surrounded by impressive voices. Professors, authors and online commentators seem far cleverer than anyone at church. Some of them openly mock faith in a crucified Savior. First Corinthians 1 was written for exactly this moment. The message of the cross has always sounded foolish to the clever. That is not evidence against it. Scripture says it is the shape God's wisdom was always going to take, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God (1 Cor 1:29).

A practical habit: When you are unsure what wisdom looks like in a situation, ask how Jesus dealt with people in the Gospels: the proud, the broken, the hostile, the curious. He is not only the source of our wisdom but its clearest picture.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul names two kinds of human demand. Some want signs: show me power and I will believe. Others want wisdom: give me an argument that satisfies my mind on my terms. God gave neither on their terms. He gave a crucified Messiah. To the proud this looks like weakness and nonsense. But to those who are called, the very same message is seen as both the power of God and the wisdom of God. What changes is not the message but the eyes. Spiritual wisdom begins when God opens our eyes to see the cross as glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice the phrase because of him. You are in Christ Jesus because of God's action, not your own cleverness. Paul has just reminded the Corinthians that not many of you were wise according to worldly standards (1 Cor 1:26). God delights to make the overlooked wise in Christ. And the four words that follow belong together: wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Christ is not only the wise teacher who shows us the way. He is the Savior who makes us right with God, makes us holy and sets us free. Wisdom that does not lead you to his cross is not the wisdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The word hidden does not mean that the treasures are locked away from believers. It means they are stored up in Christ and nowhere else, like gold in a vault, so that anyone who wants them must come to him. The Colossians were being offered spiritual experiences, special knowledge and strict rules as a way to deeper life. Paul's answer is that you cannot go deeper than Christ. Every true treasure of wisdom is already in him, and the Christian life is a lifelong exploration of what you already have.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This short verse tells us that the eternal Son of God, in his true humanity, grew. He learned as a child learns. He listened, asked questions (Luke 2:46) and increased in wisdom. Jesus did not skip the ordinary human path of growth, and so we should not despise it either. Wisdom in our own lives usually grows slowly, through years of Scripture, prayer, obedience and experience. If the sinless Son of God grew in wisdom over time, we should be patient with the slow work God is doing in us.

2.reflection:
Why do you think God chose to reveal his wisdom through something that looks as foolish as the cross?

Where are you tempted to look for wisdom outside of Christ: in experts, in experience, in popular voices, in your own instincts?

How does it encourage you that Jesus himself "increased in wisdom"? What does that say about the pace of your own growth?

Read Colossians 2:1-10. What "treasures of wisdom" in Christ do you most need to explore?

3.title: Two Ways: Wisdom and Folly
3.overview:
The Bible presents life as a road with two ways. Psalm 1 sets the blessed man, whose delight is in the law of the LORD (Ps 1:2), against the man who walks in the counsel of the wicked. Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two builders, two houses and two foundations (Matt 7:24-27). And in Proverbs 9 the choice is pictured as two women, each calling out to passers-by.

Lady Wisdom has built her house, prepared a feast and sent out her servants: Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight (Prov 9:6). Across the street the woman Folly sits at her door and calls to the same people with the same opening words, Whoever is simple, let him turn in here! (Prov 9:16). But her offer is different: Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant (Prov 9:17). Her guests do not know that the dead are there (Prov 9:18). Every day we walk down that street and hear both voices.

Proverbs gives us a cast of foolish characters so that we can recognize them in ourselves. There is the simple person, naive and easily led, open to any voice. There is the fool, who has heard the truth but prefers his own way: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes (Prov 12:15). There is the scoffer, who mocks correction and laughs at serious things. And there is the sluggard, who always has a reason not to act. The simple can still learn. The fool and the scoffer have hardened themselves against learning.

Folly is not merely silliness. At its root it is the refusal to take God into account. The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." (Ps 14:1). He may never say it with his lips. He may even attend church. But in his heart, where decisions are really made, he lives as if God were not there. That is why the Bible's call to wisdom is always also a call to repentance and faith.
3.theology:
Only two ways: Scripture does not offer a neutral middle road. Jesus said everyone who hears his words either does them or does not, and builds accordingly. Every choice we make, however small, is built on one foundation or the other.

Folly is moral, not intellectual: Biblical folly is not low intelligence. Many brilliant people are fools in the Bible's sense, and many ordinary people are wise. Folly is a heart that will not submit to God or receive correction. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (Prov 14:12).

Folly is attractive: The woman Folly is loud and seductive (Prov 9:13). Sin rarely announces itself as destruction. It offers sweetness, secrecy and pleasure now. Wisdom teaches us to look past the doorway to where the road ends.

The fool can be saved: Proverbs often speaks of fools as if they were fixed, but the gospel brings hope. Wisdom calls out How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? (Prov 1:22), and promises that those who turn at her reproof will be taught. Every wise Christian was once a fool rescued by grace. None of us began on the right road.
3.examples:
Then: Lot looked at the well-watered plain near Sodom and chose it because it looked good (Gen 13:10-11). Abraham let God choose for him. Lot's choice made perfect sense by every worldly measure, and it cost him nearly everything. Folly often looks like common sense at the moment of decision.

Now: Two friends begin their working lives at the same time. One builds habits of Bible reading, prayer, church involvement, honest work and careful spending. The other drifts: Sundays are for rest, money is for enjoying, and God can wait until life settles down. For years there is little visible difference. Both houses look fine in the sunshine. Then come the storms Jesus promised would come to both: illness, job loss, a marriage crisis, a death. The difference between the foundations finally shows.

Recognising the voices: Folly's voice today often sounds like this: "Nobody will know." "You deserve it." "Everyone else does it." "You can deal with God later." Wisdom's voice sounds like this: "God sees." "What will this lead to?" "Who will this hurt?" "Seek first his kingdom."

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table. She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says, "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Wisdom is pictured not as a stern examiner but as a generous host. She has built a house, prepared meat and wine, set the table and sent out invitations. And who is invited? Whoever is simple, and him who lacks sense. Wisdom does not wait for people to become wise before inviting them. She calls those who know they need her. This is a picture of the gospel itself. The feast of God is spread for the needy, and the only requirement is to come, eat and leave your simple ways.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing. She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town, calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says, "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Folly copies Wisdom's invitation almost word for word. She sits on the highest places of the town, just as Wisdom does, and calls the same people with the same words. Temptation rarely looks like an obvious evil. It imitates the good. But listen to what she offers: stolen water, secret bread. Her appeal is that the thing is forbidden. And she does not tell her guests the truth about her house. Sin always hides the ending. The wise person learns to ask, before going through any door, "Where does this road lead?"

verseByVerse.quote: "Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' two builders have one thing in common: both hear his words. The difference between them is not knowledge but obedience. One does them, and the other does not. This is a sobering word for people who hear many sermons and read many books. Hearing is not building. And both houses face exactly the same storm. Wisdom does not protect us from trouble. It means that when trouble comes, our lives are standing on the rock of Christ and his word, and the house does not fall.

verseByVerse.quote: The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The fool speaks in his heart. This kind of atheism is not mainly a philosophical position but a way of living. A person may believe in God in theory and yet plan, spend, speak and love as if God did not exist. The psalm then describes the result: corruption, abominable deeds and a world in which there is none who does good. Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 3 to show that all of us by nature are fools in this sense. The wise are not those who were never fools but those whom God has brought to their senses.

3.reflection:
Read Proverbs 9 aloud. What does Folly promise, and what does she hide? Where do you hear her voice most often?

Which of the foolish characters in Proverbs, the simple, the fool, the scoffer or the sluggard, do you recognize most in yourself?

Jesus' two builders both heard his words. Where are you hearing God's word without doing it?

In what area of your life might you be living as if "there is no God," even while believing in him?

4.title: How Wisdom Grows
4.overview:
No one is born wise. Wisdom has to be gained, and Scripture is clear about how God usually gives it. It grows through a few ordinary means, used faithfully over a long time.

We ask God for it. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him (Jas 1:5). James wrote this to believers in the middle of trials, who did not know how to respond. God does not scold us for asking. He gives freely. This is not a promise of new revelation, a voice or an inner impression that settles our decisions for us. It is a promise that God will give the understanding we need to walk faithfully, through his word, through others and through his guiding hand in our circumstances.

We soak ourselves in Scripture. The testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple (Ps 19:7). The sacred writings, Paul told Timothy, are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Tim 3:15). The psalmist says God's word made him wiser than his enemies, his teachers and the aged (Ps 119:98-100). A Christian who rarely opens the Bible will rarely be wise.

We walk with wise people. Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm (Prov 13:20). We become like the people we spend time with. Wisdom grows in friendship, mentoring and the life of a local church.

We welcome correction. Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid (Prov 12:1). Proverbs speaks bluntly here. Few things reveal a fool faster than how he reacts when someone tells him he is wrong.

We learn through practice and suffering. The mature have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice (Heb 5:14), and trials, James says, are part of how God makes us complete. And above all we remember that life is short: So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12).
4.theology:
God's ordinary means: God could make us wise in an instant, but he usually does not. He works through his word, prayer, the church and the experiences of life. These are not substitutes for God's work. They are how he works.

Asking in faith: James adds that we must ask in faith, with no doubting (Jas 1:6). This does not mean we must feel certain about every detail. It means we must really trust that God is good and wants to help, rather than hedging our bets between God and the world.

No new revelation needed: Scripture is sufficient to make us complete, equipped for every good work (2 Tim 3:17). Wisdom does not look for new words from heaven to settle our choices. It applies the word God has already given, with prayer, counsel and good sense, and then trusts his providence. The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Prov 16:9).

Humility is the soil: Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil (Prov 3:7). The person who thinks he is already wise has stopped growing. Wisdom grows best in people who know how much they lack.
4.examples:
Then: King Rehoboam was given two sets of advice. The older men who had served his father counselled gentleness. The young men he had grown up with urged him to be harsh. He abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him (1 Kgs 12:8). The kingdom split in two. He chose his advisers by comfort and familiarity, not by wisdom.

Now: A young couple are making a big decision about buying a house. They pray about it, which is good. But they also sit down with an older couple from church who have managed money well for decades, listen to hard questions about debt and commitments, read what Proverbs says about borrowing, and wait a month before signing. That is what asking God for wisdom usually looks like in practice: prayer joined with the word, counsel and patience.

A simple plan: Read one chapter of Proverbs a day, matching the day of the month, for a year. Pray James 1:5 each morning about one specific situation. Find one older Christian whose life you admire and ask to meet with them regularly. And the next time someone corrects you, say "Thank you" before you say anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The context is trials (Jas 1:2-4). When life is hard, we often do not know what God is doing or how to respond. James does not say, "Work it out yourself." He says, let him ask God. And look at how God gives: generously, to all and without reproach. God does not sigh at our ignorance or make us feel foolish for asking. A wise Christian is not someone who never feels lost. It is someone who knows where to go when he does, and goes often.

verseByVerse.quote: Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the aged, for I keep your precepts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist makes a bold claim. God's word made him wiser than his enemies, his teachers and the elderly. He is not boasting about his intelligence. He gives the reason each time: for it is ever with me; for your testimonies are my meditation; for I keep your precepts. The word was constantly with him, he thought about it deeply, and he obeyed it. That is the path to wisdom open to every believer, however young or ordinary. Meditation on Scripture, joined with obedience, outruns mere age and education.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most practical verses in the Bible. Our companions shape us more than we realize. The verse does not say that walking with the wise makes you feel wise, but that it makes you wise. Wisdom is caught as well as taught. And the warning is equally clear: the companion of fools will suffer harm. For parents, this verse speaks to the friendships of children. For all of us, it asks who we listen to most, whose company we seek and whose voices fill our screens.

verseByVerse.quote: But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer of Hebrews describes mature believers as those whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant practice. The picture is of an athlete whose skills have become second nature through years of training. Discernment is like that. At first you must think carefully about every choice. Over time, as you practise obeying God's word, you begin to sense quickly what is good and what is evil. There are no shortcuts. Wisdom is built one faithful decision at a time.

4.reflection:
When did you last specifically ask God for wisdom about a situation? What happened?

Read Psalm 119:97-104. What would it look like for God's word to be "ever with" you in your daily routine?

Who are the wise people you walk with? Who are the voices that most shape your thinking day to day?

How do you usually respond to correction? Think of the last time someone pointed out a fault in you.

5.title: Wise and Foolish Lives in Scripture
5.overview:
The Bible does not only teach wisdom in sayings. It shows it in lives. Its stories are full of people who acted wisely or foolishly at decisive moments, and their examples train us to recognize wisdom when we see it.

Joseph was a slave and a prisoner for years before he stood before Pharaoh. He interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, but he also gave a practical plan for surviving the famine. Pharaoh said, there is none so discerning and wise as you are (Gen 41:39). Joseph's wisdom included planning ahead, administering well and, later, forgiving his brothers with a deep understanding of God's purposes: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20).

Abigail was married to a fool. Her husband Nabal insulted David, and David set out with four hundred men to kill every male in the household. Abigail acted quickly, gathered gifts, met David on the road and spoke with humility and courage. She reminded him of God's promises and saved him from bloodguilt. David said, Blessed be your discretion (1 Sam 25:33).

Daniel, an exile in a pagan court, refused to compromise his faith, yet served the king with excellence. When the king ordered the execution of all the wise men, Daniel replied with prudence and discretion (Dan 2:14), asked for time, and went to pray with his friends.

Solomon is the Bible's great example of wisdom and its great warning. He asked God for an understanding mind to govern your people (1 Kgs 3:9), and God gave it. But when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods (1 Kgs 11:4). His wisdom did not save him from folly. And his son Rehoboam threw away the kingdom by listening to the wrong advisers. Wisdom, Scripture shows, must be kept as well as gained.
5.theology:
Wisdom in all kinds of people: Scripture's wise people include a slave who became a ruler, a wife in a hard marriage, an exile in a foreign government, a king and an unnamed woman of a besieged town who saved her city by speaking sensibly to an army commander (2 Sam 20:16-22). Wisdom is not tied to rank, gender or position. It is given to those who fear the LORD.

Wisdom and the Spirit: Pharaoh recognized in Joseph a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God (Gen 41:38). The prophet foretold that the Spirit would rest on the coming King as the Spirit of wisdom and understanding (Isa 11:2). The wisest people in Scripture are wise because God is at work in them.

Gifted wisdom is not enough: Solomon had more wisdom than anyone, yet he disobeyed the clear commands God had given about kings and their wives (Deut 17:17). Great insight did not protect a divided heart. The lesson is sobering: wisdom must be lived, not merely possessed.

All point to Christ: Each wise figure in Scripture is a partial picture. Joseph forgave and saved his brothers; Abigail stood between a wrathful king and the guilty; Daniel was faithful in exile; Solomon ruled in wisdom and peace. Christ does all of this perfectly, and never falls.
5.examples:
Abigail today: A woman finds herself between an angry husband and the neighbour he has offended. She does not shout, and she does not do nothing. She goes to the neighbour, apologizes for the wrong, brings a gift, and speaks honestly and graciously. Later, when her husband is calm, she tells him what she has done. That is the wisdom of Abigail: quick, humble, courageous and peace-making.

Daniel today: An employee is asked to take part in something dishonest at work. Rather than storming out or giving in, she asks for a meeting, proposes another way to reach the same goal honestly, and quietly prays. Like Daniel's request for vegetables (Dan 1:8-16), she looks for a respectful alternative before she has to make a stand, and is ready to make a stand if she must.

Solomon today: A gifted Bible teacher, admired for years, slowly lets small compromises grow: an unguarded friendship, a habit of private self-indulgence, a refusal to be accountable. His gifts remain, but his heart drifts. Many ministries have ended this way. Solomon's story is written so that none of us assumes our gifts will keep us faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?" Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh, a pagan ruler, saw something in Joseph that he could only explain by God. Joseph had just told him plainly, It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer (Gen 41:16). His wisdom was not self-made, and he did not claim it was. True wisdom is often visible to unbelievers. A Christian who does good work, gives sound advice and keeps calm under pressure may find, like Joseph, that people outside the church recognize that something more than human ability is at work, and that opens a door to point them to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David had been insulted, and he was about to take revenge with his own sword. Abigail stopped him. And David, to his credit, recognized God's hand in her intervention: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! Her discretion kept him from working salvation with my own hand. Two lessons stand out. Wise people make peace at personal risk. And wise people, like David here, are willing to be stopped and corrected by someone with less power than they have.

verseByVerse.quote: Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God offered Solomon anything he wanted, and Solomon asked for an understanding mind so that he could govern God's people and discern between good and evil. He did not ask for wealth, long life or the death of his enemies, and God was pleased. It is a model prayer for anyone with responsibility: parents, pastors, managers, teachers. But the rest of Solomon's story reminds us that the prayer must be prayed again and again. A heart that asked rightly when young must keep asking when old.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the saddest verses in the Old Testament. The wisest man who ever lived, apart from Christ, ended his life worshiping idols. It did not happen in a day. It happened when Solomon was old, after years of small compromises with the commands God had given. His heart was not wholly true to the LORD. Wisdom does not keep itself. It must be guarded by a whole heart, renewed daily in repentance and dependence on God. None of us is too wise to fall.

5.reflection:
Which of the wise people in this unit, Joseph, Abigail, Daniel or the wise woman of Abel, do you find most inspiring, and why?

Abigail stepped into a dangerous conflict to make peace. Is there a conflict around you that needs wise, courageous peacemaking?

What compromises might, over years, lead your heart away from the Lord the way Solomon's was?

How does each of these wise figures point forward to Christ?

6.title: Wisdom for Everyday Life
6.overview:
Much of the Bible's wisdom literature is intensely practical. Proverbs speaks about the tongue, anger, money, work, friendship, family and the heart. It is not a rulebook that answers every situation in advance. It is a training school that shapes the way we see and respond to life.

Words. A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov 15:1). Wisdom listens before it speaks: If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame (Prov 18:13). It knows when to stop: When words are many, transgression is not lacking (Prov 10:19).

Anger. Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city (Prov 16:32). Self-control is a greater victory than conquest.

Money. The borrower is the slave of the lender (Prov 22:7). Wisdom saves, plans, gives generously and avoids debt that enslaves. It counts the cost before it builds (Luke 14:28).

Work. Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise (Prov 6:6). The ant works without a supervisor and prepares for winter in summer. Wisdom is diligent, takes initiative and thinks ahead.

Friendship. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Prov 27:6). A true friend tells you the truth even when it hurts.

The heart. Beneath all of these lies the heart. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Prov 4:23). Words, anger, spending and work all flow from what we love and trust.

And Proverbs teaches one more lesson about how to use it. Two proverbs sit side by side: Answer not a fool according to his folly, and Answer a fool according to his folly (Prov 26:4-5). They do not contradict each other. They teach that wisdom must judge the situation. Sometimes answering a fool drags you down to his level; sometimes silence leaves him proud in his error. Proverbs are not mechanical laws. They are wisdom to be applied with discernment.
6.theology:
Proverbs are not promises: A proverb states how life generally works in God's world. A soft answer turns away wrath is usually true, but not every angry person will be calmed. Proverbs teaches the normal pattern of God's world, not a guarantee for every case. Reading proverbs as unbreakable promises leads to confusion and false guilt.

Wisdom from above: James describes the wisdom that comes from God: first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere (Jas 3:17). This is a portrait of wisdom's character in daily life. Set beside it the wisdom that is earthly, unspiritual, demonic, marked by bitter jealousy and selfish ambition (Jas 3:14-15). You can tell which kind is operating by its fruit.

Wise as serpents: Jesus told his disciples to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (Matt 10:16). Christian wisdom is not naive. It sees the world clearly, expects opposition, and acts shrewdly, yet without guile or sin.

Redeeming the time: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil (Eph 5:15-16). Everyday wisdom includes how we use our hours, our screens and our attention.
6.examples:
In the home: A father comes home tired and finds his teenager has broken a rule. Folly explodes immediately. Wisdom pauses, asks what happened, listens to the whole story (Prov 18:17), keeps its voice low, and deals with the matter firmly but without humiliation. The rule is upheld and the relationship survives.

Online: Someone posts an unfair attack on your faith. Folly fires back a clever, cutting reply. Wisdom asks whether a response will help or only feed the argument (Prov 26:4-5), and if it answers, answers with gentleness and respect.

With money: A family wants a new car they cannot afford. Folly signs the loan because the monthly payment seems manageable. Wisdom counts the full cost, remembers that the borrower is the slave of the lender, and keeps the old car another year while saving.

At work: A colleague takes credit for your idea. Folly broods, gossips or retaliates. Wisdom remembers that it is his glory to overlook an offense (Prov 19:11), and, if the matter is serious, raises it privately and calmly.

In friendship: A friend is making a decision that will hurt him. Folly stays silent to keep the peace. Wisdom risks the friendship to speak the truth in love, because faithful are the wounds of a friend.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This proverb is easy to memorize and hard to practise. When someone speaks to us in anger, our instinct is to answer in kind. But a harsh word is like petrol on a fire. A soft answer is not weak or dishonest. It can still say hard things. It simply says them in a tone that lowers the temperature. Many family arguments, church conflicts and workplace disputes would end quickly if one person chose to answer softly. Usually the wise person is the one who goes first.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These two verses, placed side by side on purpose, teach us how to read the whole book. Sometimes the wise thing is not to answer a fool, because arguing with him on his terms will make you like him. Sometimes the wise thing is to answer him, because silence will leave him thinking he is right. Which is it? It depends. Wisdom is not a list of rules applied without thought. It is the skill of knowing which truth fits which moment. That is why we need not only proverbs but a wise heart to use them.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sluggard is told to learn from an insect. The ant works without having any chief, officer, or ruler standing over it. It prepares in summer for what will come later. Two lessons follow. Wise people take initiative without needing someone to watch them. And wise people plan ahead, saving, preparing and working while there is opportunity. Laziness is not only a waste of time; Proverbs treats it as a form of folly that leads to poverty and shame.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James lists the marks of the wisdom that comes from God, and almost all of them are relational. It is peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy. The phrase open to reason is striking: wise people can be persuaded. They listen and change their minds when they are wrong. And the result is a harvest: a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. Wisdom is measured not by how many arguments we win but by how much peace and righteousness grows around us.

6.reflection:
Which of the six areas in this unit, words, anger, money, work, friendship or the heart, most needs God's wisdom in your life right now?

Why is it important to recognize that proverbs describe general patterns rather than guaranteed promises?

Read James 3:13-18. Which marks of "the wisdom from above" do you see growing in you, and which are missing?

Think of a recent conflict. What would a "soft answer" have looked like?

7.title: Passing Wisdom On: Parents and Children
7.overview:
Proverbs is written in the voice of a parent. Again and again it begins, My son, and it opens with a call to both parents: Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching (Prov 1:8). The book itself is wisdom being handed from one generation to the next. In chapter 4 the father even tells how he learned it: When I was a son with my father, he says, he taught me (Prov 4:3-4). Wisdom is meant to travel down the generations.

God gave Israel this responsibility from the beginning. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise (Deut 6:7). Notice where the teaching happens: at home, on the road, at bedtime and at breakfast. The main classroom for wisdom is ordinary family life. Children learn far more from what they see their parents love, fear, laugh at and pray about than from any formal lesson.

Wise parenting has two sides that must be held together. There is instruction: telling children about God, explaining why his ways are good and showing them Christ. And there is discipline: correcting, setting boundaries and letting wrong choices bring consequences. Folly is bound up in the heart of a child (Prov 22:15). Children do not drift into wisdom on their own. Yet discipline must never become harshness. Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Eph 6:4).

Above all, wise parents know their limits. They cannot give a child a new heart. Only God can do that. Their calling is to be faithful in teaching, praying and modelling the gospel, and to trust God with the outcome. And this unit is not only for parents. Grandparents, aunts and uncles, Sunday school teachers, mentors and single Christians who invest in younger believers are all passing wisdom on. Timothy's faith came first through his grandmother and mother (2 Tim 1:5), and then through Paul, who called him my true child in the faith (1 Tim 1:2).
7.theology:
Proverb, not promise: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it (Prov 22:6). As unit 6 showed, a proverb describes how life usually works in God's world, not a guarantee. Faithful parents should take great encouragement from this verse, but they should not read it as a contract. Some children of godly homes wander for years, and some never return. Their parents are not thereby proved unfaithful. Salvation is God's work, and parents rest in his sovereign grace, not in their own technique.

Discipline as love: The LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights (Prov 3:12). Discipline is a mirror of God's own fatherly care. Proverbs says that to refuse it is not kindness but neglect: Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him (Prov 13:24).

The rod: Christians read the rod passages in two main ways. Some take them as permitting measured physical discipline of young children, given calmly and in love. Others take the rod as a figure for firm correction of every kind. The first reading is the more likely as a description of what the words meant, but the heart of these verses is not the instrument. It is consistent, loving correction that does not leave a child to himself (Prov 29:15). Whatever form discipline takes, Scripture forbids anger, humiliation and harm: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged (Col 3:21).

Generations in God's purpose: Psalm 78 describes a chain of telling: fathers to children, and those children to theirs, so that they should set their hope in God (Ps 78:7). God works through families and through the church to carry the faith forward, and he delights to save from one generation to the next.
7.examples:
Then: Eli was a priest of God, yet his sons were wicked, and God judged his house because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them (1 Sam 3:13). King David did the same with his son Adonijah: His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" (1 Kgs 1:6). Adonijah grew up to grasp at his father's throne. Both men were godly in many ways, and both failed to correct their sons. Passive parenting is not gentle parenting.

Now: A family turns the evening meal into a quiet school of wisdom. Once or twice a week they read a proverb together and ask one simple question: "Where did we see this today?" A child mentions a friend who answered back angrily and made things worse. Another remembers a teacher who listened before she judged. Over the years the proverbs become part of the family's ordinary language.

When a child wanders: Parents whose grown child has turned from the faith often carry crushing guilt. Wisdom tells them three things. Confess real failures honestly to God and, where right, to the child. Refuse false guilt for the child's own choices. And keep praying, loving and leaving the door open, as the father in Jesus' parable kept watching the road (Luke 15:20).

Without children of your own: An older single woman in a church takes a teenage girl out for coffee once a month, opens Proverbs with her, and listens. Years later that girl calls her the person who taught her how to follow Christ. Passing wisdom on is not limited to biological parents.

verseByVerse.quote: And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The order matters. Before Moses tells parents to teach their children, he says, these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. Parents cannot pass on what they do not possess. A child quickly sees whether God's word is the real centre of a parent's life or only a Sunday habit. Then comes the teaching, and it is woven into all of life: sitting, walking, lying down, rising. The best family teaching is often unplanned: a conversation in the car, a question at bedtime, a prayer when bad news comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is probably the best-known verse on parenting, and it gives real hope. Early training shapes a whole life. Habits, convictions and loves formed in childhood often last into old age. Yet it is a proverb, and must be read as Proverbs itself teaches us to read: as a general truth about God's world, not a promise that cancels a child's own heart or God's sovereign choice. Parents should train with great hope, and pray with even greater dependence, knowing that only God can turn a heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul speaks to fathers, who in his world held almost unlimited power over their children, and he puts a limit on that power: do not provoke your children to anger. Constant criticism, unfair rules, broken promises, favouritism, mocking and outbursts of temper all provoke. Then he gives the positive calling: bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. The words of the Lord are crucial. Christian parents do not train children to be merely polite or successful. They raise them to know and follow Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul traces Timothy's faith back two generations, to his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Acts tells us that Timothy's father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), and there is no sign that he shared their faith. These two women passed on sincere faith in a divided home, and from childhood Timothy knew the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation (2 Tim 3:15). Their quiet faithfulness shaped one of the great leaders of the early church. No parent or grandparent who teaches a child Scripture should think the work is small.

7.reflection:
What wisdom did you receive from your own parents or other older believers? What do you wish you had been taught?

Read Deuteronomy 6:4-9. Where in your ordinary week could God's word be woven into conversation with the next generation?

Why is it important to read Proverbs 22:6 as a proverb rather than a guarantee? How does that change the way parents carry their hopes and their failures?

Eli and David both failed to correct their sons. Where are you tempted to avoid a hard but loving conversation?

Who is one younger person you could intentionally invest in, whether or not you have children of your own?

8.title: The Limits of Wisdom and the Rest of Faith
8.overview:
Proverbs teaches that life in God's world usually follows a pattern: diligence brings plenty, righteousness brings blessing, folly brings ruin. But the Bible also contains two other wisdom books that ask hard questions about that pattern. Job is about a righteous man who loses everything. Ecclesiastes is about a wise man who searches everything under the sun and finds that much of life does not add up.

Job's friends had a tidy theology. Suffering comes from sin, so Job must have sinned. They applied a true principle to the wrong situation, and God rebuked them for it (Job 42:7). Job himself questioned God, and at the end confessed, I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me (Job 42:3). The book's great poem on wisdom concludes that wisdom cannot be dug out of the earth or bought at any price. God alone knows its place, and he says to man, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding (Job 28:28).

Ecclesiastes is just as honest. The Preacher observes that in much wisdom is much vexation (Eccl 1:18). Even a wise man cannot find out what God is doing under the sun (Eccl 8:17). Good people die young; the wicked prosper; the same end comes to all. And yet the book does not end in despair. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man (Eccl 12:13).

This is the final lesson of biblical wisdom. True wisdom knows its limits. It does not claim to explain every suffering or understand every providence. It says with Paul, Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33). And then it trusts. The wisest response to what we cannot understand is not to stop believing but to rest in the God who does understand.
8.theology:
Three books, one wisdom: Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes do not contradict each other. Proverbs gives the normal pattern of God's world. Job shows that a righteous person may suffer for reasons hidden in heaven. Ecclesiastes shows that life under the sun, viewed without God, is vapour. Together they give a wisdom that is confident and humble at the same time.

Trust over understanding: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding (Prov 3:5). Even the book that most celebrates wisdom tells us not to lean on our own understanding. Wisdom finally means trusting God when we cannot trace him.

The cross as the answer to Job: Job longed for someone to stand between him and God (Job 9:33). In Christ, the righteous sufferer has come. Jesus suffered not for his own sin but for ours, and the worst event in history became the greatest good. When our suffering makes no sense, the cross assures us that God's wisdom is at work in ways we cannot yet see.

The end of the story: Ecclesiastes ends by pointing to judgment: God will bring every deed into judgment (Eccl 12:14). Life under the sun is not the whole story. The wise live in the light of eternity, numbering their days and fixing their hope on the world to come.
8.examples:
Then: Job lost his children, his wealth and his health in quick succession. His friends talked for chapters, and most of what they said sounded wise. But their wisdom had no room for mystery, and they wounded a suffering man. The wisest thing they did was at the start, when they sat with him in silence for seven days (Job 2:13).

Now: A faithful Christian couple lose a child. Well-meaning friends offer explanations: God needed another angel; everything happens for a reason you will soon see; perhaps there is sin to deal with. These words, like the words of Job's friends, are often more hurtful than helpful. Wisdom sits with the grieving, prays, brings meals and says little. It does not claim to know why. It points gently to the God who suffered in Christ, and who has promised to wipe away every tear.

When life does not add up: A diligent worker loses her job while a dishonest colleague is promoted. Proverbs might seem to have failed. Ecclesiastes says this is exactly what life under the sun looks like. Wisdom does not pretend otherwise. It keeps working honestly, trusts that God sees, and waits for the day when every deed will be judged.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Job 28 is a poem about miners digging deep into the earth for silver, gold and precious stones. Human beings can reach the darkest places of the earth, but they cannot dig up wisdom. It cannot be bought with gold. Only God knows where it is found. And when he speaks, he does not give man a secret formula. He gives a way of life: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. We may not understand everything God is doing, but we can always know what he wants us to do: fear him and turn from evil.

verseByVerse.quote: then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher had pursued wisdom harder than anyone, and this is his honest conclusion: man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. Even a wise man who claims to know cannot. This is a humbling verse for anyone who wants all the answers. Some things God has not revealed, and no amount of study will uncover them. Wisdom accepts this. It is content to know what God has revealed and to leave the rest with him (Deut 29:29).

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths. Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These well-known verses are often quoted in times of decision, but they are also about the limits of wisdom. Do not lean on your own understanding does not mean "do not think." It means do not rest your whole weight on your own understanding, as if it could carry you. Lean instead on the LORD. And the promise that he will make straight your paths is not a promise to explain everything. It is a promise to guide those who trust him, even when they cannot see far ahead. Then comes the warning: Be not wise in your own eyes. Self-confident wisdom is folly in disguise.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul has spent eleven chapters explaining the gospel and God's plan for Jews and Gentiles. And at the end of the most careful theological argument in the Bible, he does not say, "Now you understand everything." He bursts into worship at what is beyond understanding. How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! This is where all true wisdom ends: not in pride at how much we know but in praise of the God whose wisdom is infinitely greater than ours. The wisest Christian is the one most amazed by God.

8.reflection:
Have you ever applied a true principle to the wrong situation, as Job's friends did? What happened?

Read Ecclesiastes 12:9-14. How does the end of the book change the way you read the rest of it?

What situation in your life right now does not make sense? What would it look like to trust God in it?

How does the cross help you trust God's wisdom when you cannot understand his ways?

9.title: Proverbs to Memorize
9.overview:
Twenty-four proverbs, three for each of eight themes, chosen to carry the wisdom of this study into everyday life. Learn one a week and in six months you will have them all.

The fear of the LORD: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction (Prov 1:7). Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding (Prov 3:5). Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him (Prov 30:5).

Pride and humility: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Prov 16:18). When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom (Prov 11:2). Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov 28:13).

Words: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov 15:1). If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame (Prov 18:13). Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body (Prov 16:24).

Anger and self-control: Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city (Prov 16:32). Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense (Prov 19:11). Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses (Prov 10:12).

Friends and counsel: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm (Prov 13:20). Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another (Prov 27:17). Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Prov 27:6).

Money and work: Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce (Prov 3:9). The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender (Prov 22:7). Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed (Prov 19:17).

Plans and the future: Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established (Prov 16:3). Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand (Prov 19:21). Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring (Prov 27:1).

The heart and character: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Prov 4:23). A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold (Prov 22:1). The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Prov 29:25).
9.theology:
Why memorize: I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you (Ps 119:11). A proverb learned by heart is available at the moment of temptation, anger or decision, when there is no time to look anything up. Proverbs were written short so that they could be remembered.

How to read them: Remember the lessons of this study. These sayings describe how God's world usually works; they are not mechanical promises. And they all stand on the first one: wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD and is found in Christ, the wisdom of God.
9.examples:
A simple method: Write the week's proverb on a card and keep it by the kitchen sink, on the car dashboard or as the lock screen of your phone. Say it aloud each morning. By Saturday, try it without looking. Every few weeks, review the earlier ones.

Together: Learn them as a family, a couple or a small group. Children often memorize faster than adults and enjoy testing their parents. A proverb shared around the table quickly becomes part of a household's language: "Remember, a soft answer."
9.reflection:
Which theme in this list do you most need this year? Start with those three proverbs.

Which proverb do you already find yourself recalling in daily life? How has it helped you?

Who could you learn these with, so that you encourage and test one another?
